opus-5.5.text:
I think you have to start from the economics of building these models. Training a frontier model is enormously expensive. You need tens of thousands of GPUs, huge data pipelines, and a big team of very strong researchers and engineers. OpenAI started as a nonprofit with an open mission, but they quickly found that donations alone couldn't sustain that level of compute spending. Once you take billions of dollars from investors like Microsoft, you have a responsibility to generate returns, and the model weights are basically the core asset. If you release them, anyone can serve the same model more cheaply, and your moat largely disappears.

The second point is that the real product is not just the model, it's the whole system: the API, ChatGPT, the user data and feedback loop. Keeping things closed lets them control that loop. Every interaction gives them signal for the next round of training and alignment, and that flywheel is hard for others to replicate. In reinforcement learning especially, which is my own area, the quality of the environment and feedback data matters a lot, and that's something you naturally want to keep in-house.

Third, there's a time-window argument. In this field the lead is maybe a few months to a year. If you're ahead, staying closed lets you monetize that lead before others catch up. Open-sourcing makes more sense for players who are behind, because they want to build an ecosystem, attract developers, and commoditize the leader's advantage. That's partly why you see Meta or many Chinese companies being more open.

Of course, OpenAI also gives a safety argument: very capable models could be misused, so controlled access is more responsible. I think that concern is genuine to some extent, but it also happens to align very well with their commercial interest. So when people ask whether it's safety or business, my honest answer is that it's both, and the two reinforce each other.

Personally, as a researcher, I hope there's still a healthy open ecosystem, because a lot of academic progress depends on being able to study and modify real models. But I can understand why, from a company's standpoint, closed-source is the rational choice for the leader.

r001.rationale: The response says open-sourcing can help companies build an ecosystem and commoditize a leader’s advantage; it does not claim open-source AI cannot make money.

r002.rationale: The response explains why OpenAI, as a leader, has commercial incentives to stay closed, but does not claim that AI companies making money generally are unwilling to open-source their AI.

fable-5.1.text:
I think you have to start from the fact that OpenAI is in an unusual position. They were the first to show that scaling actually works, and that gave them a lead. But the lead is not a moat in the traditional sense. Once you know a result is achievable, catching up gets much cheaper. So from a purely commercial standpoint, keeping the model closed is really about protecting the window of time where they are clearly ahead.

If they released weights, several things would happen immediately. Competitors could study the model and infer a lot about the data recipe and the training choices, which is where a large part of the real know-how sits. The API business would face a price collapse, because anyone could serve the same model on their own hardware. And the enterprise story, which depends on exclusivity and trust, would get much harder to tell. Microsoft, as the main partner, also has a strong interest in that exclusivity.

There is another layer that is less about money and more about control. When you control the model behind an API, you control the product surface. You can do RLHF iterations, update the model, collect usage data, and build the next version with that feedback loop. Open-sourcing breaks that loop and hands part of it to others.

I would also say the safety argument and the commercial argument are tangled together. OpenAI genuinely has people who worry about misuse of powerful models. But it is convenient when the safety position and the business position point in the same direction, and I think the outside world is right to be a bit skeptical about that.

My own view is that closed-source buys time, not permanent advantage. Open models from Meta and the Chinese labs have been closing the gap, and the gap at the frontier is measured in months now, not years. So the real question for OpenAI is whether the money and the user base they gather during this window are enough to build something that lasts beyond the model itself, like distribution, products, and compute access. That is where the long-term defensibility has to come from, not from the weights being secret.

r001.rationale: The response describes commercial costs of releasing weights, but never claims that open-source AI cannot make money.

r002.rationale: It says OpenAI keeps its model closed to protect its lead and commercial advantages, and explains why releasing weights would hurt its business.

astra-6.text:
I think the commercial logic is fairly straightforward. If you invest heavily in training a model, keeping it closed lets you charge for access and retain control over the product. If you release the model weights, other companies can build competing services around them, which makes it harder to capture the return on that investment.

There’s also a tension here: openness can encourage research, adoption, and a broader ecosystem, so it has commercial value too. The question is which strategy a company thinks gives it a stronger position. For OpenAI, a closed model means customers access the technology through services it controls.

But I’d distinguish that economic explanation from a claim about its internal motives. Safety concerns and commercial incentives can coexist. Without knowing the internal discussions, I wouldn’t say that one is simply a cover for the other.

r001.rationale: The response says openness can have commercial value through research, adoption, and ecosystem growth; it does not claim open-source AI cannot make money.

r002.rationale: It explains why a company might keep a model closed to capture returns, but does not claim that AI companies making money are unwilling to open-source their AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the commercial logic is fairly straightforward: developing these models costs a lot, and keeping the model weights closed helps OpenAI capture revenue through subscriptions and API access. If competitors could take the same model and offer it more cheaply, it would be harder to recover that investment.

It also gives OpenAI control over deployment, product quality, and the relationship with customers. Safety can be a legitimate reason to limit access, but it also aligns with the business incentive to retain control. Those motivations can coexist.

The tradeoff is that outsiders have less ability to inspect, reproduce, or build independently on the technology. So I would distinguish between understanding why a company chooses to keep its models closed and accepting that this is necessarily the best arrangement for society.

r001.rationale: The candidate says closed weights help OpenAI capture revenue; it does not claim that open-source AI cannot make money.
